question: Why are living organisms classified?
solution: Classification is necessary to study the enormous diversity of life systematically. It helps in (i) identification and naming of organisms, (ii) understanding relationships among organisms, (iii) easy and efficient communication — a name identifies the same organism worldwide, (iv) predicting properties of unknown organisms based on their classified relatives.

question: Why are classification systems changing every now and then?
solution: Classification systems change because (i) new organisms are constantly being discovered, (ii) advances in technology (electron microscopy, molecular biology, DNA sequencing) reveal new information about structure and evolutionary relationships, and (iii) criteria for classification are refined as our understanding of phylogeny improves.

question: What different criteria would you choose to classify people that you meet often?
solution: People could be classified by: (i) physical features — height, build, eye colour, skin colour; (ii) language spoken; (iii) nationality/region of origin; (iv) age group; (v) occupation; (vi) educational background. The choice of criteria depends on the purpose of classification.

question: What do we learn from identification of individuals and populations?
solution: Identification of individuals and populations helps us understand (i) specific characteristics distinguishing one species from another, (ii) the range of variation within a species, (iii) geographic distribution and ecological roles, and (iv) evolutionary relationships and biodiversity patterns.

question: Define a taxon. Give some examples of taxa at different hierarchical levels.
solution: A taxon (pl. taxa) is a unit of any taxonomic rank used in biological classification. Examples: Kingdom Plantae (highest rank shown), Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Primata, Family Hominidae, Genus Homo, Species Homo sapiens. Each taxon represents a grouping of organisms sharing common characteristics.

question: Can you identify the correct sequence of taxonomical categories? (a) Species→Order→Phylum→Kingdom (b) Genus→Species→Order→Kingdom (c) Species→Genus→Order→Phylum
solution: Option (c) Species→Genus→Order→Phylum is correct. The correct ascending hierarchy is: Species < Genus < Family < Order < Class < Phylum/Division < Kingdom. Option (a) skips Genus/Family; option (b) reverses Species and Genus.

question: Define: (i) Phylum (ii) Class (iii) Family (iv) Order (v) Genus
solution: Phylum (Division in plants): a major taxonomic category between Kingdom and Class, grouping organisms with the same body plan (e.g., Phylum Chordata). Class: category between Phylum and Order (e.g., Class Mammalia). Family: category between Order and Genus grouping closely related genera (e.g., Family Felidae). Order: category between Class and Family, grouping related families (e.g., Order Carnivora). Genus: category immediately above Species, grouping closely related species sharing many characters (e.g., Genus Panthera).

question: Discuss how classification systems have undergone several changes over a period of time.
solution: Early classification: Aristotle used simple morphological characters (plants: herbs/shrubs/trees; animals: air/land/water dwellers). Two-Kingdom system (Linnaeus, 18th c.): Plantae and Animalia — problematic for unicellular organisms. Three-Kingdom (Haeckel, 1866): added Protista. Four-Kingdom: added Monera for prokaryotes. Five-Kingdom (Whittaker, 1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — based on cell type, body organisation, nutrition, reproduction. Modern: Six-Kingdom (separating Eubacteria and Archaebacteria) and Three-Domain system (Woese) based on rRNA sequences.

question: State two economically important uses of: (a) heterotrophic bacteria (b) archaebacteria
solution: (a) Heterotrophic bacteria: (i) used in making curd, cheese, vinegar and antibiotics (e.g., Streptomyces, Lactobacillus); (ii) saprophytic bacteria decompose dead organic matter, recycling nutrients essential for soil fertility. (b) Archaebacteria: (i) methanogens like Methanobacterium produce biogas (methane) from cattle dung — an economical fuel source; (ii) thermoacidophiles are studied for enzymes (e.g., Taq polymerase from thermophilic archaebacteria) used in biotechnology (PCR).

question: What is the nature of cell-walls in diatoms?
solution: Diatoms have cell walls (frustules) made of silica (hydrated silicon dioxide, SiO2·nH2O). The frustules are composed of two overlapping halves (epitheca and hypotheca) that fit together like a soap box. These siliceous walls are indestructible and accumulate over geological time as diatomaceous earth (kieselguhr), used as a filtering agent and mild abrasive.

question: How are viroids different from viruses?
solution: Viroids (discovered by T.O. Diener, 1971): are free, circular single-stranded RNA molecules with no protein coat; very small (~250-400 nucleotides). Viruses: have a protein coat (capsid) enclosing nucleic acid (DNA or RNA); larger and structurally more complex. Viroids cause diseases such as potato spindle tuber disease; they replicate using host-cell enzymes without encoding any protein.
steps: Viroids: RNA only, no protein coat, naked circular ssRNA
Viruses: nucleic acid + protein coat (capsid), ± envelope
Viroid example: potato spindle tuber viroid (PSTVd)

question: Describe briefly the four major groups of Protozoa.
solution: 1. Amoeboid (Rhizopoda): move and capture prey using pseudopodia; free-living in soil/water or parasitic (Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery). 2. Flagellated (Mastigophora): have one or more flagella; free-living or parasitic (Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness; Leishmania causes kala-azar). 3. Ciliated (Ciliata/Infusoria): have numerous cilia for locomotion and feeding; mostly free-living (Paramoecium has a gullet). 4. Sporozoans (Apicomplexa): have an infective spore-like stage; all are parasitic (Plasmodium causes malaria).

question: What do the terms phycobiont and mycobiont signify?
solution: In lichens (a symbiotic association): Phycobiont — the photosynthetic partner, usually a green alga or cyanobacterium; it produces food by photosynthesis. Mycobiont — the fungal partner; it provides shelter, minerals and water, and absorbs moisture. The two organisms together form a lichen thallus that can grow in extreme habitats neither partner could survive alone.

question: What are the characteristic features of Euglenoids?
solution: Euglenoids (e.g., Euglena): (i) freshwater organisms found in stagnant water; (ii) have no cell wall but a flexible protein-rich pellicle; (iii) bear two flagella (one short, one long for locomotion); (iv) contain photosynthetic pigments (chlorophylls a, b) so they are photoautotrophs in light and heterotrophs in darkness; (v) have an eyespot (stigma) sensitive to light; (vi) reserve food is paramylon (a unique polysaccharide); (vii) reproduce by longitudinal binary fission.

question: Give a brief account of viruses with respect to their structure and nature of genetic material. Also name four common viral diseases.
solution: Structure: Viruses are non-cellular particles with an outer protein coat (capsid) made of capsomeres and an inner core of nucleic acid. Some animal viruses have a lipid bilayer envelope. Shape: polyhedral, helical, or complex (bacteriophage). Genetic material: either DNA (single- or double-stranded) or RNA (single- or double-stranded), never both. RNA viruses (retroviruses) can convert RNA→DNA via reverse transcriptase. Four common viral diseases: (i) Influenza (RNA virus), (ii) Dengue (RNA/flavivirus), (iii) HIV/AIDS (retrovirus), (iv) Common cold (rhinovirus).

question: What is the basis of classification of algae?
solution: Algae are classified primarily on the basis of: (i) type of photosynthetic pigments (e.g., chlorophyll a/b in Chlorophyceae; chlorophyll a/c + fucoxanthin in Phaeophyceae; chlorophyll a/d + phycoerythrin in Rhodophyceae); (ii) nature and chemistry of reserve food (starch in green algae, laminarin/mannitol in brown algae, floridean starch in red algae); (iii) type of flagella (number, position, structure); (iv) cell wall chemistry.

question: When and where does reduction division (meiosis) take place in the life cycle of a liverwort, a moss, a fern, a gymnosperm and an angiosperm?
solution: Liverwort/Moss (bryophytes): meiosis occurs in the sporophyte capsule (sporangium) to form haploid spores — sporic meiosis. Fern (pteridophyte): meiosis in sporangia on the underside of fronds (sori) to produce haploid spores. Gymnosperm: meiosis in microsporangia (pollen mother cells → microspores) and in megasporangia (megaspore mother cell → megaspores) within the ovule. Angiosperm: meiosis in anthers (microsporogenesis) and in ovule nucellus (megasporogenesis). In all seed plants meiosis is thus confined to reproductive organs.

question: Mention the ploidy of the following: protonemal cell of a moss; primary endosperm nucleus in dicot; leaf cell of a moss; prothallus cell of a fern; gemma cell in Marchantia; meristem cell of monocot; ovum of a liverwort; zygote of a fern.
solution: Protonemal cell of moss: n (haploid — part of gametophyte). Primary endosperm nucleus in dicot: 3n (triploid — formed by fusion of two polar nuclei + one sperm). Leaf cell of moss: n (haploid — gametophyte). Prothallus cell of fern: n (haploid — gametophyte). Gemma cell in Marchantia: n (haploid — vegetative propagule from gametophyte). Meristem cell of monocot: 2n (diploid — sporophyte). Ovum of liverwort: n (haploid). Zygote of fern: 2n (diploid — first cell of sporophyte).

question: What are the difficulties that you would face in classification of animals, if common fundamental features are not taken into account?
solution: Without fundamental features, classification would be: (i) superficial — based only on appearance (colour, size), leading to unrelated animals being grouped together; (ii) inconsistent — different biologists arriving at different groupings; (iii) unable to reflect evolutionary relationships; (iv) unable to predict shared physiology, biochemistry or behaviour. For example, bats and birds both fly but have very different fundamental features — without body plan criteria they might be incorrectly grouped.

question: How useful is the study of the nature of body cavity and coelom in the classification of animals?
solution: The nature of coelom is a fundamental criterion: (i) Acoelomates (e.g., Platyhelminthes) — no body cavity; organs embedded in mesoderm. (ii) Pseudocoelomates (e.g., Aschelminthes) — body cavity not lined by mesoderm (pseudocoelom). (iii) Coelomates (e.g., Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Chordata) — true coelom lined by mesoderm (peritoneum). Coelom provides space for organ development, acts as a hydrostatic skeleton, and is essential for circulation in some groups — it reflects major evolutionary divergences.

question: Distinguish between intracellular and extracellular digestion.
solution: Intracellular digestion: food particles are engulfed by phagocytosis into food vacuoles within cells; digestion occurs inside the cell by lysosomal enzymes. Seen in Porifera (sponges) and some Coelenterates. Extracellular digestion: enzymes are secreted into a digestive cavity (gut lumen) where food is broken down outside cells; more efficient for large food particles. Seen in most higher animals from Coelenterates to Chordates. The two may coexist in some organisms (e.g., Hydra).

question: What is the difference between direct and indirect development?
solution: Direct development: the juvenile (hatched/born form) resembles the adult and grows directly into an adult without a larval stage or metamorphosis (e.g., lizards, birds, mammals, earthworms). Indirect development: the hatched form is a larva, morphologically and ecologically distinct from the adult; it undergoes metamorphosis (a series of developmental changes) to reach the adult form. Examples: frog (tadpole → frog), butterfly (caterpillar → pupa → butterfly), sea urchin (pluteus larva). Indirect development increases exploitation of different ecological niches.

question: Water vascular system is the characteristic of which group? (a) Porifera (b) Ctenophora (c) Echinodermata (d) Chordata
solution: Answer: (c) Echinodermata. The water vascular system (ambulacral system) is unique to echinoderms. It is a hydraulic network of fluid-filled canals connected to tube feet (podia) used for locomotion, food capture, and gas exchange. Water enters through the madreporite → stone canal → ring canal → radial canals → tube feet. Examples: starfish, sea urchin, sea cucumber.

question: 'All vertebrates are chordates but all chordates are not vertebrates.' Justify.
solution: Phylum Chordata is characterised by three features at some stage of life: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, and paired pharyngeal gill slits. Vertebrates (Subphylum Vertebrata) are chordates where the notochord is replaced by a vertebral column. However, there are non-vertebrate chordates: Subphylum Urochordata (tunicates — notochord only in larval tail) and Subphylum Cephalochordata (Amphioxus/lancelets — notochord throughout life but no vertebral column). Hence all vertebrates have chordate features but not all chordates have a vertebral column.

question: Segmentation in the body is first observed in which of the following: (a) Platyhelminthes (b) Aschelminthes (c) Annelida (d) Arthropoda
solution: Answer: (c) Annelida. Annelids (e.g., earthworm Lumbricus, Nereis) are the first phylum to show true metamerism — the body is divided into repeated segments (metameres) each containing a set of organs. This metameric segmentation is internally reflected in serial repetition of coelom, ganglia, blood vessels and nephridia. Arthropoda and Chordata are more derived phyla that also show segmentation but have it modified/fused.

question: How is a pinnately compound leaf different from a palmately compound leaf?
solution: Pinnately compound leaf: the leaflets are arranged on either side of a common central axis (rachis) — resembles a feather. The rachis is an extension of the petiole. Example: neem (Azadirachta indica), Rose. Palmately compound leaf: all leaflets arise from a single point at the tip of the petiole, like fingers from a palm. There is no rachis. Example: Silk cotton (Bombax ceiba), Cannabis. The key distinction is the presence (pinnate) or absence (palmate) of a rachis.

question: Explain with suitable examples the different types of phyllotaxy.
solution: Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves on a stem. Types: (i) Alternate: one leaf per node on alternating sides (e.g., China rose, mustard, sunflower). (ii) Opposite: two leaves per node, opposite each other (e.g., Calotropis, guava). Within opposite, if successive pairs are at right angles, it is called decussate (e.g., Coleus). (iii) Whorled: three or more leaves at each node arranged in a whorl around the stem (e.g., Alstonia, Nerium).

question: Describe the various types of placentations found in flowering plants.
solution: Placentation is the arrangement of ovules on the placenta inside the ovary. Types: (i) Marginal: placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture; ovules borne on this ridge — bean, pea (monocarpellary, unilocular). (ii) Axile: ovary multi-locular; ovules on the central axis where septa meet — tomato, lemon (syncarpous). (iii) Parietal: ovules on the inner wall or on intruding false septa of a unilocular ovary — mustard, Argemone. (iv) Free central: ovules on a central column; no septa — Dianthus, Primrose. (v) Basal: single ovule at the base of a unilocular ovary — sunflower, marigold.

question: What is a flower? Describe the parts of a typical angiosperm flower.
solution: A flower is the reproductive shoot of an angiosperm, modified for sexual reproduction. Parts: (i) Calyx: outermost whorl of sepals (green, protective in bud); may be gamosepalous (fused) or polysepalous (free). (ii) Corolla: petals, attract pollinators; may be gamopetalous or polypetalous. (iii) Androecium: male reproductive organs — stamens each consisting of filament + anther (contains pollen). (iv) Gynoecium (pistil): female reproductive organs — carpels each with stigma, style, ovary (contains ovules). The thalamus is the modified stem on which all whorls are borne.

question: Cut a transverse section of young stem of a plant from your school garden and observe it under a microscope. How would you ascertain whether it is a monocot stem or a dicot stem?
solution: Dicot stem: (i) vascular bundles arranged in a ring around a central pith; (ii) bundles are conjoint, collateral and open (cambium present between xylem and phloem); (iii) distinct cortex and pith regions; (iv) well-developed bundle sheath of parenchyma. Monocot stem: (i) vascular bundles scattered throughout the ground tissue (no distinct cortex/pith boundary); (ii) bundles are conjoint, collateral and closed (no cambium); (iii) each bundle surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath; (iv) no secondary growth. The scattered arrangement of bundles with sclerenchymatous sheaths and absence of cambium distinguishes a monocot stem.

question: A transverse section shows: (a) vascular bundles conjoint, scattered, surrounded by sclerenchymatous bundle sheaths; (b) phloem parenchyma absent. What would you identify it as?
solution: These are characteristic features of a monocot stem. Scattered conjoint vascular bundles with sclerenchymatous bundle sheaths and absent phloem parenchyma are diagnostic of stems of grass-like monocots (e.g., maize/Zea mays, sugarcane). The absence of phloem parenchyma and the presence of protective sclerenchyma around bundles are key identifying features.

question: Name the three basic tissue systems in flowering plants. Give the tissue names under each system.
solution: 1. Epidermal tissue system: epidermis (single layer), stomata (guard cells + epidermal cells), trichomes (stem hairs), root hairs. 2. Ground tissue system: parenchyma (cortex, pith, mesophyll), collenchyma (hypodermis in dicot stems, angles), sclerenchyma (fibres, sclereids — provide strength). 3. Vascular tissue system: xylem (tracheids, vessel elements, xylem parenchyma, xylem fibres) and phloem (sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres).

question: How is the study of plant anatomy useful to us?
solution: Plant anatomy is useful for: (i) identifying plant species and adulterants in plant-based drugs/food (pharmacognosy); (ii) understanding wood structure — density, grain, properties — for timber/furniture selection; (iii) crop improvement — knowledge of stem/leaf anatomy helps breed plants with better water-use efficiency; (iv) palaeobotany — fossil plant anatomy gives evolutionary insights; (v) fibre quality assessment (e.g., jute, cotton, hemp fibres) for textile/paper industries.

question: Mention the function of the Ureters in frog.
solution: In frogs, the ureters serve dual roles: (i) carry urine from the kidneys to the cloaca for excretion; (ii) in males, they also serve as vas deferens — carrying sperms from the testes to the cloaca (hence called urinogenital ducts in male frogs). This dual reproductive/excretory function is a characteristic of amphibian anatomy.

question: Which of the following is NOT correct? (a) Robert Brown discovered the cell (b) Schleiden and Schwann formulated cell theory (c) Virchow explained that cells form from pre-existing cells (d) A unicellular organism carries out life activities within a single cell
solution: Answer: (a) Robert Brown did NOT discover the cell. The cell was first observed by Robert Hooke (1665) in cork. Robert Brown (1831) discovered the nucleus. Statements (b), (c), and (d) are correct — Schleiden and Schwann proposed cell theory (1838-39), Virchow added 'Omnis cellula e cellula' (1855), and unicellular organisms are indeed self-sufficient.

question: New cells generate from: (a) bacterial fermentation (b) regeneration of old cells (c) pre-existing cells (d) abiotic materials
solution: Answer: (c) pre-existing cells. This is the principle added by Rudolf Virchow to cell theory — 'Omnis cellula e cellula' (every cell from a pre-existing cell). Cells arise only by division of existing cells. Life does not arise de novo from abiotic materials (which would be spontaneous generation, now disproved).

question: Which of the following is correct? (a) Cells of all living organisms have a nucleus. (b) Both animal and plant cells have a well defined cell wall. (c) In prokaryotes, there are no membrane-bound organelles. (d) Cells are formed de novo from abiotic materials.
solution: Answer: (c) In prokaryotes, there are no membrane-bound organelles. Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi, etc.) — this is their defining feature. (a) is false — prokaryotes lack a true nucleus; (b) is false — animal cells have no cell wall; (d) is false — Virchow's principle states cells arise from pre-existing cells.

question: What is a mesosome in a prokaryotic cell? Mention the functions that it performs.
solution: Mesosome: an infolding (invagination) of the plasma membrane in prokaryotic cells, forming vesicles, tubules or lamellae. Functions: (i) increases the surface area of the plasma membrane, aiding cellular respiration (similar to mitochondrial cristae functionally); (ii) plays a role in DNA replication and segregation during cell division — the mesosome is attached to the chromosome; (iii) aids in secretion of cell wall-synthesising enzymes; (iv) may function in formation of the cell plate during cell division.

question: What are the characteristics of prokaryotic cells?
solution: Prokaryotic cells: (i) lack a membrane-bound nucleus — DNA is in a nucleoid region (not enclosed by a nuclear membrane); (ii) no membrane-bound organelles (no mitochondria, ER, Golgi, chloroplasts); (iii) ribosomes are 70S (50S + 30S subunits), smaller than eukaryotic 80S; (iv) cell wall usually present (peptidoglycan in bacteria, pseudopeptidoglycan in some archaea); (v) may have plasmids (extra-chromosomal circular DNA); (vi) may have flagella with a different structure (hollow, rigid) from eukaryote flagella; (vii) much smaller (1–10 µm) than most eukaryotic cells.

question: What are nuclear pores? State their function.
solution: Nuclear pores are large protein complexes (~120 nm diameter) that perforate the double nuclear envelope at sites where both inner and outer membranes fuse. They are formed by nucleoporins arranged in an octagonal symmetry. Functions: (i) selective bidirectional transport — mRNA and tRNA exit the nucleus; ribosomal subunits exit; (ii) proteins (transcription factors, DNA/RNA polymerases, histones) enter the nucleus; (iii) maintain nucleo-cytoplasmic traffic essential for gene expression; small molecules (<40 kDa) diffuse freely through pores.

question: Both lysosomes and vacuoles are endomembrane structures, yet they differ in terms of their functions. Comment.
solution: Lysosomes: membrane-bound organelles containing hydrolytic enzymes (acid hydrolases) synthesised in the ER and packaged by the Golgi. Function: intracellular digestion — digest macromolecules, old organelles (autophagy), and foreign material (heterophagy); involved in programmed cell death. Vacuoles: membrane-bound (tonoplast) sacs containing water, cell sap, storage products, waste materials. Function: primarily storage and turgor maintenance in plant cells (central vacuole occupies up to 90% of cell volume); osmoregulation in freshwater protists (contractile vacuole). Lysosomes are digestive organelles; vacuoles are storage/regulatory organelles.

question: What are macromolecules? Give examples.
solution: Macromolecules are large, high-molecular-weight molecules (>10,000 Da) found in the acid-insoluble fraction of cells. They are polymers of smaller monomeric units. Examples: (i) Proteins — polymers of amino acids; structural (keratin, collagen), enzymatic (amylase), transport (haemoglobin). (ii) Polysaccharides — polymers of monosaccharides; starch (storage in plants), glycogen (storage in animals), cellulose (structural in plants). (iii) Nucleic acids — DNA (polymer of deoxyribonucleotides) and RNA (polymer of ribonucleotides). (iv) Lipids (specifically phospholipids forming membranes) are sometimes included although not strictly polymers.

question: What is meant by tertiary structure of proteins?
solution: Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional folding of an entire polypeptide chain (which may already have secondary structure elements like alpha-helices and beta-sheets) into a compact, specific 3D shape. It is stabilised by: (i) disulphide bonds (between cysteine residues), (ii) hydrogen bonds (between –OH, –NH, –COOH groups), (iii) hydrophobic interactions (non-polar side chains cluster in core away from water), (iv) electrostatic/ionic interactions (between charged side chains), (v) van der Waals forces. The tertiary structure determines the protein's specific biological activity — particularly important for enzyme active sites.

question: Explain the composition of triglyceride.
solution: A triglyceride (triacylglycerol) is a lipid consisting of: (i) one molecule of glycerol (a trihydric alcohol, C3H8O3) esterified with (ii) three molecules of fatty acids. The ester bond (–CO–O–) forms between the –OH of glycerol and the –COOH of each fatty acid via condensation with loss of water. Fatty acids may be saturated (no double bonds, e.g., palmitic, stearic) or unsaturated (one or more C=C, e.g., oleic, linoleic). The three fatty acids in a natural triglyceride may be the same (simple triglyceride) or different (mixed triglyceride).

question: Describe the important properties of enzymes.
solution: Important properties of enzymes: (i) They are mostly proteins (some RNA molecules act as ribozymes); (ii) are catalysts — increase reaction rate without being consumed; (iii) are highly specific — each enzyme acts on a specific substrate (lock-and-key / induced-fit model); (iv) are required in small quantities (turnover number can be very high — one enzyme molecule may catalyse thousands of reactions/second); (v) activity is affected by temperature (optimal ~37°C for most human enzymes) and pH (each has an optimal pH); (vi) can be inhibited (competitive or non-competitive inhibition); (vii) may require cofactors/coenzymes for activity; (viii) do not change the equilibrium of a reaction, only speed its attainment; (ix) are denatured by high temperature or extreme pH.

question: What is the average cell cycle span for a mammalian cell?
solution: The average cell cycle span for a typical mammalian cell growing in culture is approximately 24 hours. Of this, most time is spent in interphase (~23 hours: G1 ~11 h, S-phase ~8 h, G2 ~4 h) and only about 1 hour in M-phase (mitosis + cytokinesis). Actual duration varies greatly by cell type — some cells divide every few hours; others (like neurons) are permanently arrested in G0 and never divide in an adult.

question: Distinguish cytokinesis from karyokinesis.
solution: Karyokinesis: division of the nucleus — includes all stages of mitosis or meiosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) in which the chromosomes are divided and distributed equally to two daughter nuclei. Cytokinesis: division of the cytoplasm — follows karyokinesis; the cell splits into two daughter cells. In animals: a cleavage furrow forms by actomyosin ring contraction. In plants: a cell plate (phragmoplast) forms from vesicles between the daughter nuclei and grows centrifugally to become the new cell wall. Karyokinesis without cytokinesis produces multinucleate cells (coenocytes/syncytia).

question: Describe the events taking place during interphase.
solution: Interphase is the metabolically active, non-dividing phase of the cell cycle comprising three sub-phases: G1 (Gap 1): cell grows in size, synthesises RNA and proteins, prepares for DNA synthesis; cell is metabolically active; restricted point (R-point) determines commitment to divide. S-phase (Synthesis): DNA replication occurs — each chromosome is duplicated, forming sister chromatids joined at the centromere; DNA content doubles (2N→4N in diploid cells); histone synthesis also occurs. G2 (Gap 2): further cell growth, synthesis of proteins needed for mitosis (tubulins for spindle), continued RNA and protein synthesis; organelle duplication; cell checks for complete, error-free DNA replication before entering M-phase.

question: What is G0 (quiescent phase) of cell cycle?
solution: G0 (quiescent/dormant phase): some cells, after completing mitosis, exit the cell cycle and enter a non-dividing state called G0. These cells remain metabolically active but do not prepare for or undergo further cell division. G0 cells have withdrawn from the cell cycle and may remain in this state temporarily (e.g., liver cells — can re-enter on injury) or permanently (e.g., mature neurons, red blood cells). The G0 state represents cellular quiescence or terminal differentiation, controlled by growth factor withdrawal and CDK inhibitors.

question: By looking at a plant externally, can you tell whether a plant is C3 or C4? Why and how?
solution: In most cases, NO — external morphology alone is not sufficient to reliably distinguish C3 from C4 plants. However, some clues: C4 plants are often grasses from tropical/subtropical regions (e.g., maize, sugarcane, sorghum) while most temperate plants are C3. Some C4 plants may show slightly more erect, waxy or narrower leaves. However, these are not definitive — confirmation requires anatomical observation (Kranz anatomy) or biochemical tests (δ13C values). External appearance is insufficient for a definitive identification.

question: By looking at which internal structure of a plant can you tell whether it is C3 or C4?
solution: The definitive internal structure is Kranz anatomy, seen in transverse sections of leaves of C4 plants. In C4 plants: (i) bundle sheath cells surrounding vascular bundles are large, have thick walls, no intercellular spaces, and contain numerous large chloroplasts with well-developed grana and starch granules; (ii) mesophyll cells are arranged in a concentric ring around the bundle sheath (radiate arrangement). In C3 plants: bundle sheath cells are small, thin-walled, lack chloroplasts (or have few) and do not form a prominent concentric ring. This distinctive two-celled arrangement (mesophyll + bundle sheath) with chloroplast-rich bundle sheaths identifies a C4 plant.

question: Even though very few cells in a C4 plant carry out the biosynthetic (Calvin) pathway, yet they are highly productive. Can you explain why?
solution: C4 plants are highly productive because: (i) CO2 is first fixed in mesophyll cells by PEP carboxylase (high affinity for CO2, not inhibited by O2) forming a 4-carbon acid (OAA → malate/aspartate); (ii) this 4-carbon compound is transported to bundle sheath cells where it is decarboxylated, releasing CO2 at high concentrations around Rubisco in the bundle sheath; (iii) this CO2 concentration mechanism suppresses photorespiration (Rubisco oxygenase activity) — in C3 plants up to 25% of fixed carbon is lost via photorespiration; (iv) C4 plants thus use Rubisco more efficiently for carboxylation; (v) this is especially advantageous in hot, sunny, dry conditions where stomata close and CO2 becomes limiting for C3 plants.

question: Differentiate between: (a) Respiration and Combustion; (b) Glycolysis and Krebs' cycle; (c) Aerobic respiration and Fermentation
solution: (a) Respiration vs Combustion: Respiration is a biological, enzymatically controlled, stepwise oxidation of organic molecules releasing energy gradually as ATP + heat; occurs at body temperature. Combustion is rapid, uncontrolled oxidation releasing all energy as heat and light at once; requires high activation energy. (b) Glycolysis vs Krebs' cycle: Glycolysis occurs in cytoplasm; converts 1 glucose→2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP + 2 NADH; no CO2 released. Krebs' cycle occurs in mitochondrial matrix; oxidises acetyl-CoA through 8 steps releasing 2CO2/turn, producing 3 NADH + 1 FADH2 + 1 GTP per turn; substrate-level phosphorylation. (c) Aerobic respiration vs Fermentation: Aerobic uses O2 as terminal electron acceptor; completely oxidises glucose to CO2 + H2O; yields ~36-38 ATP. Fermentation is anaerobic; pyruvate is converted to ethanol+CO2 (yeast) or lactate (muscle/bacteria); only 2 ATP produced; NAD+ regenerated without O2.

question: What are respiratory substrates? Name the most common respiratory substrate.
solution: Respiratory substrates are organic molecules that are oxidised during cellular respiration to release energy. Types: (i) Carbohydrates — most common; glucose is the most preferred and most common respiratory substrate. (ii) Fats (fatty acids) — highest energy yield/gram but require more O2. (iii) Proteins — amino acids (after deamination) can enter glycolysis or Krebs' cycle. (iv) Organic acids (intermediates). The most common respiratory substrate is glucose (C6H12O6), which is the primary substrate for glycolysis.

question: What are the main steps in aerobic respiration? Where does each take place?
solution: Aerobic respiration has three main stages: (i) Glycolysis: in the cytoplasm — glucose→2 pyruvate; net 2 ATP + 2 NADH. (ii) Pyruvate oxidation and Krebs' cycle (Citric Acid Cycle): in the mitochondrial matrix — pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA by pyruvate dehydrogenase (1 NADH + 1 CO2 each); acetyl-CoA enters Krebs' cycle producing 3 NADH + 1 FADH2 + 1 GTP per turn. (iii) Electron Transport System (ETS) + Oxidative Phosphorylation: in the inner mitochondrial membrane — NADH and FADH2 are oxidised via protein complexes (I, II, III, IV); proton gradient drives ATP synthase; O2 is the final electron acceptor (→H2O). Overall: 1 glucose → ~36-38 ATP.

question: What are the assumptions made during the calculation of net gain of ATP?
solution: The theoretical calculation of ~36-38 ATP per glucose assumes: (i) all NADH produced in glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation and Krebs' cycle enters the mitochondrial ETS; (ii) each mitochondrial NADH yields ~2.5 ATP; each FADH2 yields ~1.5 ATP (or traditionally 3 and 2); (iii) each cytoplasmic NADH (from glycolysis) yields ~1.5–2 ATP due to the cost of transporting electrons across the inner mitochondrial membrane (malate-aspartate or glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle); (iv) the entire process operates under ideal, standard conditions; (v) no energy is lost to proton leak or heat. In practice, actual ATP yield per glucose in living cells is lower (~30 ATP).

question: Discuss: 'The respiratory pathway is an amphibolic pathway.'
solution: An amphibolic pathway is one that serves both catabolic (breaking down) and anabolic (building up) functions. Respiration is traditionally catabolic — it degrades glucose to release energy. However, many intermediates of the respiratory pathway are drawn off for biosynthesis: (i) pyruvate → amino acid alanine; (ii) oxaloacetate → aspartate; (iii) α-ketoglutarate → glutamate; (iv) acetyl-CoA → fatty acid synthesis; (v) glucose-6-phosphate → pentose phosphate pathway (ribose-5-P for nucleotides). Conversely, biosynthetic precursors can enter respiration (amino acids deaminated and fed to Krebs' cycle). Thus the pathway serves dual metabolic roles — hence amphibolic.

question: Define RQ. What is its value for fats?
solution: Respiratory Quotient (RQ) = volume of CO2 released / volume of O2 consumed (at the same temperature and pressure) during the oxidation of a given substrate. For carbohydrate (glucose): C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O; RQ = 6/6 = 1.0. For fats: fats are more reduced (high H:O ratio) so more O2 is needed to fully oxidise them, releasing proportionally less CO2. For a typical fat (e.g., tripalmitin): RQ ≈ 0.7. For proteins: RQ ≈ 0.9. For organic acids: RQ > 1 (e.g., malic acid RQ ≈ 1.33). RQ < 1 indicates fat/protein oxidation; RQ = 1 indicates carbohydrate oxidation.

question: Define growth, differentiation, development, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation, determinate growth, meristem and growth rate.
solution: Growth: irreversible permanent increase in size/mass of an organism. Differentiation: process by which cells derived from meristems mature and acquire specific structural and functional characteristics. Development: the totality of changes undergone by an organism including growth, differentiation, and morphogenesis. Dedifferentiation: phenomenon where differentiated cells regain meristematic activity (e.g., formation of interfascicular cambium from parenchyma). Redifferentiation: dedifferentiated cells lose meristematic activity and again become specialised (e.g., secondary phloem/xylem from cambium). Determinate growth: growth that ceases after reaching a genetically fixed size (most animals, leaves). Meristem: plant tissue with dividing cells at tips/lateral positions (apical, lateral, intercalary). Growth rate: amount of growth per unit time.

question: Why is not any one parameter good enough to demonstrate growth throughout the life of a flowering plant?
solution: Different parameters measure different aspects of growth: (i) fresh weight changes with water content and can fluctuate; (ii) dry weight (organic matter) increases monotonically but requires destructive sampling; (iii) length/height applies to elongating organs but not to compact/bulky organs; (iv) number of cells is relevant for early growth (embryo) but impractical to measure in a whole plant; (v) leaf area applies to shoot photosynthetic surface but not to roots. At different stages (germination, vegetative, reproductive, seed filling) different parameters are most informative. Thus, no single parameter captures the whole story of growth throughout a plant's life.

question: Why is abscisic acid also known as stress hormone?
solution: Abscisic acid (ABA) is called the stress hormone because it is synthesised and released in response to environmental stresses: (i) Water stress (drought): ABA triggers stomatal closure (by causing K+ efflux from guard cells, reducing turgor), thus reducing water loss through transpiration — the most rapid and well-known response. (ii) Cold stress: ABA accumulates and induces cold hardiness. (iii) ABA promotes seed dormancy — seeds resist germination in unfavourable conditions. (iv) ABA promotes leaf and fruit abscission under stress. Because its accumulation increases dramatically during adverse environmental conditions and it mediates adaptive responses, it is called the stress/dormin hormone.

question: Which PGR would you use if you are asked to: (a) induce rooting in a twig (b) quickly ripen a fruit (c) delay leaf senescence (d) induce growth in axillary buds (e) bolt a rosette plant (f) induce immediate stomatal closure
solution: (a) Rooting in a twig: Auxin (IBA — indole-3-butyric acid); promotes adventitious root formation. (b) Quickly ripen a fruit: Ethylene; triggers fruit ripening and softening. (c) Delay leaf senescence: Cytokinin; delays chlorophyll degradation and nutrient mobilisation (Richmond-Lang effect). (d) Induce growth in axillary buds: Cytokinin; promotes lateral bud growth by overcoming apical dominance imposed by auxin. (e) Bolt a rosette plant: Gibberellin; causes bolting (rapid internode elongation followed by flowering). (f) Induce immediate stomatal closure: Abscisic acid (ABA); triggers guard cell K+ efflux → loss of turgor → stomatal closure.

question: Define vital capacity. What is its significance?
solution: Vital Capacity (VC): the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation (or inspired after a maximum exhalation). VC = IRV + TV + ERV (Inspiratory Reserve Volume + Tidal Volume + Expiratory Reserve Volume). Normal value: ~4600 mL in males, ~3400 mL in females. Significance: (i) measures the functional reserve of the lungs; (ii) reduced VC indicates restrictive lung disease (pulmonary fibrosis, pleural effusion) or respiratory muscle weakness; (iii) used to assess lung health and monitor respiratory disease progression; (iv) reflects the maximum ventilation capacity available for exercise.

question: State the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal breathing.
solution: After a normal, quiet exhalation, the volume of air remaining in the lungs is the Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) = Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) + Residual Volume (RV) = ~1100 + ~1200 = ~2300 mL. The air that cannot be expelled even by maximum forced exhalation is the Residual Volume (~1200 mL). This residual air keeps the alveoli from completely collapsing and ensures continuous gas exchange between breaths.

question: What are the major transport mechanisms for CO2? Explain.
solution: CO2 is transported from tissues to lungs by three mechanisms: (i) Dissolved in plasma: ~7% of CO2 is transported simply dissolved. (ii) As bicarbonate (HCO3–): ~70% — in RBCs, CO2 combines with water (catalysed by carbonic anhydrase) to form H2CO3, which ionises to H+ and HCO3–; HCO3– moves out into plasma (chloride shift — Cl– moves in); in lungs the reverse occurs. (iii) Carbamino compounds: ~23% — CO2 binds directly to amino groups of haemoglobin's protein moiety (not the haem group) forming carbaminohaemoglobin; released in lungs where lower pCO2 dissociates the compound.

question: Explain the process of inspiration under normal conditions.
solution: Inspiration (inhalation) is an active process: (i) The diaphragm contracts and flattens (moves downward, increasing thoracic volume vertically). (ii) External intercostal muscles contract, lifting the ribs upward and outward (increasing thoracic volume antero-posteriorly and laterally). (iii) Thoracic volume increases → intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure (from 760 to ~758 mmHg). (iv) Air flows in along the pressure gradient (atmosphere → lungs) until pressures equalise. During deep inspiration, accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, scalene) also contract to elevate the ribs further.

question: What is the effect of pCO2 on oxygen transport?
solution: Increased pCO2 (and resultant decreased pH — the Bohr effect) reduces haemoglobin's affinity for O2, causing more O2 to be released from oxyhaemoglobin. Mechanistically: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3–; the H+ ions bind to haemoglobin causing conformational change that shifts the O2-dissociation curve to the right (lower O2 saturation at the same pO2). This is advantageous at metabolically active tissues where pCO2 is high — more O2 is delivered. Conversely, in the lungs where pCO2 is low and pH is higher, haemoglobin readily binds O2.

question: Define oxygen dissociation curve. Can you suggest any reason for its sigmoidal pattern?
solution: Oxygen dissociation curve: a graph plotting percentage saturation of haemoglobin (y-axis) against pO2 (x-axis). It is S-shaped (sigmoidal). Reason for sigmoidal shape: Haemoglobin has four subunits; binding of O2 to one subunit induces cooperative conformational changes (allostery/positive cooperativity) that increase the affinity of remaining subunits for O2. This means: at low pO2 (tissue level), Hb has lower affinity (easy O2 release); at higher pO2 (lung level), binding of initial O2 makes subsequent binding progressively easier, giving the steep rise at intermediate pO2. This cooperative binding produces the S-shape rather than a simple hyperbola.

question: Name the components of the formed elements in the blood and mention one major function of each.
solution: Formed elements are the cellular components of blood suspended in plasma: (i) Red Blood Cells (Erythrocytes): contain haemoglobin; primary function is O2 and CO2 transport. (ii) White Blood Cells (Leukocytes): 5 types: neutrophils (phagocytosis of bacteria), eosinophils (allergic responses, parasite defence), basophils (release histamine in allergies), monocytes (phagocytosis, become macrophages), lymphocytes (immune response — B-cells produce antibodies, T-cells cell-mediated immunity). (iii) Platelets (Thrombocytes): non-nucleated cell fragments; essential for blood clotting (coagulation) by aggregating at wound sites and releasing clotting factors.

question: What is the importance of plasma proteins?
solution: Plasma proteins (albumin, globulins, fibrinogen) serve several vital roles: (i) Osmotic balance: albumin (most abundant) maintains colloidal osmotic (oncotic) pressure, preventing fluid leakage from capillaries into tissues. (ii) Immunity: gamma globulins (immunoglobulins/antibodies) neutralise pathogens. (iii) Clotting: fibrinogen is converted to fibrin — forms the clot mesh. (iv) Transport: albumin and specific globulins transport lipids, hormones, ions, drugs. (v) Buffering: proteins act as pH buffers. (vi) Viscosity: contribute to blood viscosity (important for normal flow).

question: Why do we consider blood as a connective tissue?
solution: Blood is classified as a connective tissue because: (i) it has a matrix (plasma — extracellular, fluid) in which cells are suspended — the characteristic feature of connective tissue; (ii) it originates from mesoderm (mesenchyme), like all other connective tissues; (iii) it connects and integrates the body — transporting materials (O2, CO2, nutrients, hormones, waste) between organs; (iv) it has specialised cells suspended in a non-cellular matrix (plasma), analogous to collagen-producing cells in loose connective tissue. Though liquid, blood shares the fundamental connective tissue structure of cells + extracellular matrix.

question: What is meant by double circulation? What is its significance?
solution: Double circulation: blood passes through the heart twice per complete circuit: (i) Pulmonary circulation: right heart → lungs → left heart (deoxygenated blood is oxygenated). (ii) Systemic circulation: left heart → body tissues → right heart (oxygenated blood delivers O2; returns deoxygenated). Significance: (i) keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood completely separate (no mixing in a 4-chambered heart) unlike fish (single circulation); (ii) allows high-pressure systemic circulation (left ventricle pumps at higher pressure) while maintaining lower-pressure pulmonary circulation — preventing pulmonary oedema; (iii) supports high metabolic rates seen in warm-blooded (homeothermic) mammals and birds.

question: Why do we call our heart myogenic?
solution: The heart is called myogenic (Gr. myo = muscle, genic = originating) because the heartbeat is initiated by the cardiac muscle itself — it is self-excitable (autorhythmic). The sino-atrial node (SA node), a specialised patch of nodal tissue in the right atrium, spontaneously generates the electrical impulse that triggers each heartbeat without any neural input. In contrast, neurogenic hearts (e.g., some crustaceans) require a nerve impulse to initiate each beat. Even an isolated, denervated mammalian heart continues to beat rhythmically because the SA node is intrinsic to the cardiac muscle.

question: Sino-atrial node is called the pacemaker of our heart. Why?
solution: The SA node is called the pacemaker because: (i) it spontaneously depolarises at the highest inherent rate (~70-80 times/min at rest) of all cardiac autorhythmic cells; (ii) this rate is faster than the AV node (~40-60/min) or Purkinje fibres (~20-40/min), so the SA node always drives the heart rate; (iii) the electrical impulse generated by the SA node propagates through atria, causing atrial contraction, then reaches the AV node and coordinates ventricular contraction; (iv) the SA node thus sets the pace for the entire heart — hence 'pacemaker'.

question: Define a cardiac cycle and the cardiac output.
solution: Cardiac cycle: the sequence of events — electrical, mechanical, and valvular — constituting one complete heartbeat from one beat to the next. It consists of: systole (contraction of atria, then ventricles) followed by diastole (relaxation). Duration of one cardiac cycle at 72 beats/min ≈ 0.8 s (atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, joint diastole 0.4 s). Cardiac output (CO): the volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per minute. CO = Heart Rate × Stroke Volume. Normal: 72 beats/min × 70 mL/beat ≈ 5040 mL/min (~5 L/min). CO increases dramatically during exercise (up to 20-25 L/min in athletes).

question: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
solution: Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR): the amount of filtrate produced by the kidneys per minute. Normal GFR in a healthy adult is approximately 125 mL/min (or ~180 L/day). GFR is determined by the net filtration pressure (hydrostatic pressure of blood in glomerulus minus the osmotic pressure of plasma proteins and the capsular pressure), and by the filtration surface area. Almost all of the filtrate is reabsorbed — only ~1.5–2 L of urine is excreted daily.

question: Explain the autoregulatory mechanism of GFR.
solution: GFR is autoregulated by the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) via the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS): (i) If GFR falls, reduced flow in the distal convoluted tubule is detected by the macula densa cells. (ii) Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells (modified smooth muscle in afferent arteriole) secrete renin. (iii) Renin converts angiotensinogen→angiotensin I→angiotensin II. (iv) Angiotensin II (a potent vasoconstrictor) constricts the efferent arteriole, increasing glomerular pressure and GFR back to normal; also stimulates aldosterone release from adrenal cortex, promoting Na+ reabsorption and water retention, increasing blood volume and pressure.

question: Indicate whether the following statements are true or false and correct the false ones.
solution: a) Micturition is carried out by a reflex: TRUE — micturition (urination) is a reflex initiated when bladder stretch receptors signal the spinal cord; though voluntary control modifies it via the cerebral cortex. b) ADH helps in water elimination making urine hypotonic: FALSE — ADH (antidiuretic hormone/vasopressin) increases water reabsorption in collecting ducts, making urine concentrated (hypertonic), not dilute. c) Protein-free fluid is filtered from blood plasma into Bowman's capsule: TRUE — the glomerular filtration barrier retains plasma proteins; the filtrate is similar to plasma but protein-free. d) Henle's loop plays an important role in concentrating urine: TRUE — the countercurrent mechanism in Henle's loop creates a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium essential for concentrating urine. e) Glucose is actively reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule: TRUE — all filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed in the PCT by sodium-glucose co-transporters (active transport).

question: Give a brief account of the counter current mechanism.
solution: The countercurrent mechanism creates a concentration gradient in the renal medulla enabling urine concentration: (i) Descending limb of Henle's loop: permeable to water, impermeable to solutes; water moves out into the hypertonic interstitium → tubular fluid becomes progressively concentrated toward the loop bend. (ii) Ascending limb: impermeable to water, actively transports NaCl out → interstitium becomes hyperosmotic; tubular fluid becomes dilute. (iii) The parallel loops of Henle (countercurrent multiplier) and vasa recta capillaries (countercurrent exchanger) together maintain the osmotic gradient from cortex (~300 mOsm) to inner medulla (~1200 mOsm). (iv) When ADH is present, collecting duct becomes permeable to water, which moves out into the hyperosmotic medulla, concentrating the urine.

question: Explain micturition.
solution: Micturition (urination): the process of voiding urine from the bladder. When urine accumulates (~200-400 mL), stretch receptors in the bladder wall are stimulated → afferent signals travel to the micturition centre in the spinal cord (S2-S4) → parasympathetic efferent signals cause detrusor muscle contraction and internal urethral sphincter relaxation → urge to void is signalled to the cerebral cortex. Voluntary control from the cortex relaxes the external urethral sphincter (skeletal muscle under somatic control) → urine flows out. In infants and spinal cord injuries, micturition is purely a reflex (involuntary).

question: Define sliding filament theory of muscle contraction.
solution: The sliding filament theory (Huxley and Hanson, 1954) states that muscle contraction occurs due to the sliding of thin (actin) filaments over thick (myosin) filaments, with no change in the length of the filaments themselves. During contraction: (i) Myosin heads (using ATP) bind to actin, undergo a power stroke (pivot), and slide actin filaments toward the M-line; (ii) the H-zone and I-band narrow/disappear; (iii) the A-band width remains constant; (iv) sarcomere shortens → muscle shortens. The filaments themselves do not contract; the sarcomere's length decreases because filaments slide past each other.

question: Describe the important steps in muscle contraction.
solution: Steps: (i) Nerve impulse reaches neuromuscular junction → acetylcholine released → end-plate potential → action potential propagates along sarcolemma and T-tubules. (ii) T-tubules signal the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release Ca2+ ions into the sarcoplasm. (iii) Ca2+ binds troponin (on the thin filament), causing tropomyosin to shift and expose the myosin-binding sites on actin. (iv) Energised myosin heads (ADP + Pi bound) attach to actin → cross-bridge formation. (v) Power stroke: myosin head pivots, ADP + Pi released → thin filaments slide toward M-line. (vi) New ATP binds myosin → cross-bridge detaches; ATP hydrolysis re-energises the head. (vii) Cycle repeats as long as Ca2+ and ATP are available. (viii) When nerve stimulation stops, Ca2+ is pumped back into SR → tropomyosin re-covers binding sites → relaxation.

question: Briefly describe the structure of the Brain.
solution: The human brain is enclosed in the skull (cranium) and covered by three meninges (dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater). Major regions: (i) Forebrain: Cerebrum (largest, two hemispheres with cerebral cortex — seat of intelligence, memory, voluntary control; corpus callosum connects hemispheres), thalamus (relay centre for sensory signals), hypothalamus (temperature regulation, hunger, water balance, links nervous and endocrine systems), olfactory lobes. (ii) Midbrain (Mesencephalon): corpora quadrigemina (visual and auditory reflexes); connects forebrain and hindbrain; cerebral peduncles. (iii) Hindbrain: Pons (relay, respiratory regulation), Medulla oblongata (controls involuntary functions — heart rate, breathing, swallowing), Cerebellum (coordination of voluntary movement, balance, posture).

question: Compare: (a) Central neural system (CNS) and Peripheral neural system (PNS); (b) Resting potential and action potential
solution: (a) CNS: consists of brain and spinal cord; processes and integrates information; protected by skull/vertebral column and meninges; communicates via nerve impulses. PNS: all nervous tissue outside the CNS — cranial nerves (12 pairs), spinal nerves (31 pairs), ganglia; divided into somatic NS (voluntary, controls skeletal muscle) and autonomic NS (involuntary, controls smooth muscle, cardiac, glands). PNS relays sensory signals to CNS and motor commands from CNS to effectors. (b) Resting potential: the electrical potential across the unstimulated neuron membrane; inner surface negative relative to outer (–70 mV); maintained by Na+/K+ ATPase pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in) and K+ leak channels; outside high Na+/low K+, inside low Na+/high K+. Action potential: when stimulated, Na+ channels open → Na+ rushes in → depolarisation (potential rises to ~+35 mV); then K+ channels open → K+ exits → repolarisation; brief hyperpolarisation before return to resting; propagates along nerve fibre as a wave (all-or-none).

question: Explain: (a) Polarisation of the membrane; (b) Depolarisation; (c) Transmission of a nerve impulse across a chemical synapse
solution: (a) Polarisation: the resting state of a neuron membrane where the inside is electrically negative (–70 mV) relative to outside. Maintained by: Na+/K+ pump actively pumping 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in; K+ leak channels (membrane more permeable to K+); fixed negative charges inside (proteins). Result: outside is positive (high Na+), inside is negative (high K+). (b) Depolarisation: when a stimulus exceeds threshold, voltage-gated Na+ channels open rapidly → Na+ floods into the cell → inside becomes positive (reversal of polarity, reaching ~+35 mV); this constitutes the rising phase of the action potential. (c) Chemical synapse transmission: action potential reaches presynaptic terminal → voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open → Ca2+ influx → synaptic vesicles (containing neurotransmitter) fuse with presynaptic membrane → neurotransmitter (e.g., acetylcholine, noradrenaline) is released by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft → diffuses across cleft → binds to receptors on postsynaptic membrane → ion channels open → generates a new electrical signal (EPSP or IPSP) in the postsynaptic neuron.

question: Define: (a) Exocrine gland (b) Endocrine gland (c) Hormone
solution: (a) Exocrine gland: a gland that secretes its product through a duct to the target site (outside the bloodstream). Examples: salivary glands (saliva into mouth), sweat glands (sweat to skin surface), pancreatic acini (digestive enzymes into the duodenum). (b) Endocrine gland (ductless gland): secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream (no duct); hormones travel to target organs via blood. Examples: thyroid, pituitary, adrenal cortex. Some glands are both (e.g., pancreas — endocrine islets of Langerhans + exocrine acini). (c) Hormone: a chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland/cell, transported via blood, and acting on specific target cells/organs at low concentrations to regulate physiological functions. Chemically, hormones may be peptides, steroids, or amino acid derivatives.

question: List the hormones secreted by: Hypothalamus, Pituitary, Thyroid, Parathyroid, Adrenal, Pancreas
solution: Hypothalamus: releasing hormones (GnRH, TRH, CRH, GHRH, PRH) and inhibiting hormones (GnIH/somatostatin, PIH/dopamine); also ADH and oxytocin (released from posterior pituitary). Pituitary (anterior): GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, Prolactin, MSH; posterior: ADH, oxytocin (produced by hypothalamus). Thyroid: T3 (triiodothyronine), T4 (thyroxine) — regulate BMR; calcitonin (lowers blood calcium). Parathyroid: PTH (parathyroid hormone) — raises blood calcium (stimulates osteoclasts, kidney Ca2+ reabsorption, vitamin D activation). Adrenal cortex: glucocorticoids (cortisol), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), sex steroids (androgens). Adrenal medulla: epinephrine (adrenaline), norepinephrine. Pancreas — alpha cells: glucagon (raises blood glucose); beta cells: insulin (lowers blood glucose).

question: Write short notes on the functions of: (a) PTH (b) Thyroid hormones (c) Thymosins (d) Androgens (e) Estrogens (f) Insulin and Glucagon
solution: (a) PTH: secreted by parathyroid in response to low blood Ca2+; raises Ca2+ by stimulating bone resorption (osteoclast activation), increasing Ca2+ reabsorption in kidney, and activating vitamin D (which enhances intestinal Ca2+ absorption). (b) Thyroid hormones (T3, T4): regulate basal metabolic rate; essential for normal growth (especially brain development in foetus/infant); increase oxygen consumption and heat production; regulate protein, fat, carbohydrate metabolism. (c) Thymosins: peptide hormones from thymus; promote differentiation of T-lymphocytes; important for cell-mediated immunity and also stimulate antibody production. (d) Androgens (mainly testosterone): produced by testicular Leydig cells; control male reproductive organ development, secondary sexual characters (voice, beard, muscle mass), spermatogenesis, libido. (e) Estrogens (mainly estradiol): produced by ovarian follicles; control female secondary sexual characters, endometrial proliferation, menstrual cycle; important in pregnancy. (f) Insulin: secreted by beta cells when blood glucose rises; promotes glucose uptake (GLUT4 insertion), glycogenesis, protein/lipid synthesis — hypoglycemic. Glucagon: secreted by alpha cells when blood glucose falls; stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis — hyperglycemic. Together they maintain blood glucose homeostasis.

question: Which hormonal deficiency is responsible for: (a) Diabetes mellitus (b) Goitre (c) Cretinism
solution: (a) Diabetes mellitus: deficiency of insulin (Type 1 — absolute deficiency; Type 2 — relative deficiency/insulin resistance). Result: hyperglycemia, glucosuria, osmotic diuresis, weight loss. (b) Goitre: deficiency of dietary iodine → insufficient thyroxine synthesis → low T3/T4 → high TSH (via negative feedback removal) → TSH stimulates thyroid growth → enlarged thyroid (goitre). Can also occur due to excess iodine or thyroid pathology. (c) Cretinism: deficiency of thyroid hormones (T3/T4) in infancy/childhood. Results in severely stunted physical and mental development — short stature, intellectual disability, coarse features, delayed sexual maturation. Early detection (neonatal screening) and T4 replacement can prevent these effects.

question: Briefly mention the mechanism of action of FSH.
solution: FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone) is a glycoprotein hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary. Mechanism: (i) FSH binds to specific G-protein-coupled receptors on target cells (ovarian granulosa cells in females, Sertoli cells in males). (ii) Receptor activation stimulates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP production → PKA activation → phosphorylation of regulatory proteins. (iii) In females: FSH promotes growth and maturation of ovarian follicles, stimulates granulosa cells to produce estradiol (via aromatase induction), and coordinates the menstrual cycle. (iv) In males: FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis — stimulates production of androgen-binding protein (ABP) and inhibin. FSH thus acts through a classic cAMP second-messenger cascade.
